subject: CartGrid pilot — throughput validation & SLO next steps
messages:
From: Priyom Das <priyom_das@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Green <alex@cartgrid.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
Date: Sun, 14 Feb 2027 15:12:00 -0800
Subject: CartGrid pilot — throughput validation & SLO next steps

Hi Alex — thanks again for the call today. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we can size the pilot and lock SLA targets. I pulled the key numbers you shared and added a few clarifying asks below.

Summary of what we heard on the call:
- Workload shape: heavy burst activity tied to checkout events. Baseline steady-state is ~120 QPS (small requests), with burst crests hitting 3,800 QPS for ~30–90s during promotions.
- Typical payload: average request ~220 tokens; 95th token length ~620 tokens when additional metadata is included.
- Streaming: a subset (~15%) of sessions require streaming responses (progressive summarization during async checkout flows). Those sessions expect sub-250ms per-chunk latency and ability to maintain 20 concurrent streaming sessions per region.
- Latency target: customer-facing p95 generation latency <= 450ms for non-streaming, with p50 around 120–160ms for common requests.

Redwood ops considerations / gaps we flagged:
- For the crest behavior we'll recommend a mixed approach: Dedicated reserved slots for baseline + autoscaling burst capacity with short-term burst credit — need to confirm acceptable cold-start behavior and fallback model for crest overflow.
- KV/prefix caching expected to reduce effective tokens/sec for repeated contexts; we'll propose an initial caching profile after we see the sample traffic.

Actions / asks (proposed, please confirm):
1) Please send a 48–72h representative sample of traffic (anonymized) — ideally NDJSON of request timestamps, token counts, streaming flag, and any concurrency grouping. We need this to produce tokens/sec and crest-duration histograms. (Attachment stub: cartgrid_sample_traffic.json)
2) Confirm the acceptable p95 latency window (is 450ms acceptable across regions or do we need tighter SLAs for specific flows?).
3) Let us know if encryption/KMS requirements or network egress restrictions will require Private deployment for the pilot.
4) Proposed next call: ops + engineering sync to review the traffic snapshot and Redwood's preliminary sizing — options Tue/Wed 10:00–12:00 PT.

Deliverables from Redwood after we get the sample:
- A short throughput profile (tokens/sec and QPS heatmap), peak vs. sustained capacity recommendation, and an initial cost estimate for Hosted vs Dedicated pilot.
- A draft SLO table (p50/p95 targets, streaming chunk latency, concurrency limits) — attached as redwood_slo_proposal_v1.pdf.

If you can drop the sample in reply, we’ll run the profiling job and share results within 48 business hours.

Thanks — Priyom

Thanks, Priyom — helpful recap. A few clarifications:
- The 3,800 QPS crest is real and tied to marketing blasts; crest windows are typically 45–75 seconds.
- Peak token counts happen when we include full cart context + third-party pricing metadata (that's the ~620 token 95th).
- Streaming sessions are server-push style where we send incremental product recommendations. Concurrency for streaming could spike to ~35 in the worst promotions if multiple users open the checkout at the same time in the same region. We should plan for safe headroom.

We'll anonymize and upload a 72-hour sample to the drive link below by EOD today. One ask from our side: can Redwood include an expected degradation mode description (what happens if crest exceeds capacity — queued requests, fallback to smaller model, or throttling)? We want to align on user experience tradeoffs.

Great context — thanks Alex. Adding a little ops color from Redwood side and proposed options for degradation behavior so we can align before the sizing run.

Short answers up front:
- Degradation modes we recommend (configurable per route):
  1) Graceful fallback to a smaller, cheaper model family (fewer tokens, faster kernels) for overflow when latency budgets are tight — best for preserving user-facing throughput with slightly lower output fidelity.
  2) Queueing with short TTL (e.g., 4s) for non-interactive background tasks — preserves correctness but increases tail latency.
  3) Token-aware shedding: prioritize requests by token-length/importance, drop or reject very large non-critical requests during crest windows.

What Redwood will deliver after we process your sample:
- QPS and tokens/sec heatmaps, crest-duration CDF, and a recommended slot/instance mix (Dedicated + burst policy) to meet the 450ms p95 target for primary flows.
- A streaming concurrency plan (we'll show how many dedicated streaming workers are needed to keep per-chunk latency <250ms at target concurrency).
- A short runbook snippet describing degradation order (fallback model -> short queue -> shed) and UX implications for each.

Small request: when you upload the sample, include a flag per event for 'critical' vs 'background' so we can model priority preserving. If that's not possible, mark checkout/confirm flows as critical so we model them conservatively.

I'll block time for Tue 16 Feb 10:30 PT for a 45-min ops sync unless you prefer the earlier window. Priyom will run the profiling once the sample is in the folder.

Thanks — Marissa
